patient.chief_complaint: New progressive motor weakness with muscle fasciculations superimposed on known behavioral FTD
patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. M is a 67-year-old man with a diagnosis of behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) made 18 months ago based on personality change, disinhibition, executive dysfunction, and hypometabolism on FDG-PET in frontal and temporal regions. He has been managed with behavioral interventions and medications.

Over the past 6-7 months, his wife has noticed NEW motor symptoms: progressive bilateral arm weakness with visible muscle wasting of his hands, muscle twitching in his arms and calves, slurring of speech that is beyond his prior FTD-related dysexecutive speech pattern, and what appears to be tongue wasting. He has had difficulty with feeding himself and has had episodes of choking.

The diagnostic question is whether this patient has: (1) ALS-FTD — the most common overlap syndrome, caused in ~40% of cases by C9orf72 expansion, where both ALS and FTD occur in the same patient, (2) Pure FTD progression with an independent motor finding, or (3) Another etiology (paraneoplastic, prion disease).

The family history of a father who died of a 'nervous system disease' at age 62 raises concern for familial C9orf72 ALS-FTD. The clinical picture of combined cognitive-behavioral syndrome (bvFTD) and motor neuron disease (ALS features) is the classic ALS-FTD presentation.

output.query: ALS-FTD C9orf72 expansion clinical features management

results.title: C9orf72 ALS-FTD: clinical spectrum and management
results.finding: C9orf72 expansion is the most common cause of both familial ALS (~40%) and familial FTD (~25%). About 15% of all ALS patients have behavioral/cognitive FTD features. ALS-FTD is a unified disease of TDP-43 proteinopathy. Prognosis is worse than either condition alone.

results.title: Management of ALS-FTD
results.finding: ALS-directed pharmacotherapy as used in isolated ALS is continued in the ALS-FTD population. Behavioral symptoms associated with frontotemporal dementia are typically managed with SSRIs and low-dose antipsychotics. Published guidelines recommend early assessment of decision-making capacity in patients with concurrent cognitive impairment.

output.summary: C9orf72 hexanucleotide expansion is the most common single genetic cause of both familial ALS and familial FTD. The co-occurrence of motor neuron disease and frontotemporal dementia defines the ALS-FTD spectrum. Neurofilament light chain levels are markedly elevated in ALS-FTD compared with isolated ALS or FTD. Clinical correlation recommended.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: ALS-FTD (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with frontotemporal dementia), C9orf72 pathogenic expansion

differential.key_features: No DWI cortical ribboning, no thalamic involvement, RT-QuIC negative, 14-3-3 negative. CJD progresses over weeks-months; this course is slower.
FTD does not cause fasciculations, LMN EMG changes, or the pure motor weakness pattern seen here. Motor involvement requires ALS diagnosis.
Full paraneoplastic panel pending — no obvious primary tumor; C9orf72 genetic confirmation explains presentation without invoking paraneoplastic syndrome

critical_actions: RT-QuIC and 14-3-3 in CSF — CJD must be excluded before ALS-FTD diagnosis, as treatment and prognostic implications differ dramatically
C9orf72 genetic testing — most important single test in patient with combined ALS and FTD features
Advance care planning URGENTLY with surrogate — FTD impairs decision-making; decisions about NIV, PEG, and code status must be made now
ECG before riluzole — quetiapine-riluzole QTc interaction
Genetic counseling for family: each first-degree relative has 50% risk of C9orf72 expansion
contraindicated_actions: Diagnosing behavioral changes as FTD progression without investigating new motor findings
Initiating ALS treatment without assessing decision-making capacity — patient may lack capacity to consent to treatment
Starting riluzole without ECG baseline given concurrent quetiapine
key_reasoning_points: ALS-FTD is the most severe presentation in the ALS spectrum. C9orf72 expansion is the single most important genetic test when both ALS and FTD co-occur.
Prion disease (CJD) must be urgently excluded because it is the most important rapid progressive dementia + motor neuron disease mimic — RT-QuIC has >96% sensitivity for prion disease.
Decision-making capacity is critically impaired in FTD — advance care planning must begin immediately with legal surrogate (spouse). Cannot defer this.
NfL in ALS-FTD is the highest of any neurodegenerative condition (>10,000 pg/mL common) — reflecting combined cortical and motor neuron degeneration.

red_herrings.data_point: Known behavioral variant FTD (bvFTD) diagnosed 18 months ago — new motor symptoms attributed to FTD progression
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute new motor weakness to FTD progression (FTD can cause motor features in some variants) rather than recognizing superimposed ALS
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: bvFTD does not cause fasciculations, LMN EMG changes, or tongue atrophy. New motor symptoms in FTD require ALS investigation. C9orf72 expansion explains combined syndrome.

red_herrings.data_point: Quetiapine use — antipsychotic can cause metabolic and neurological side effects
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute muscle weakness to quetiapine-related metabolic myopathy or drug effect
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Quetiapine at 25 mg does not cause progressive motor neuron disease with fasciculations and LMN denervation. ALS is the diagnosis.

metadata.notes: ALS-FTD with pathogenic C9orf72 expansion. Most complex ALS case: combined motor neuron disease and FTD; prion disease must be excluded urgently; decision-making capacity impaired by FTD; QTc monitoring required for drug interactions.
